area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: In adults treated in hospital for an acute migraine attack, what proportion receive an opioid?
why: Opioids do not treat migraine and increase the risk of medication overuse headache and re-attendance, yet they remain a common emergency analgesic. No audit of opioid use in acute migraine has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG150 rec 1.3.16 (2012, guideline updated June 2025)
standard.wording: Do not offer ergots or opioids for the acute treatment of migraine.

pass: No opioid (codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol, morphine, oxycodone or others) given in hospital or prescribed on discharge for the migraine attack.
population: Adults (18+) attending the emergency department or acute medical unit with a discharge diagnosis of migraine. Exclude secondary headache diagnoses and patients on long-term opioids for another condition.
sample: 40 consecutive coded migraine attendances over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: ED and acute medical unit coding for migraine; electronic prescribing and drug administration record; discharge prescription.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a migraine order set to the ED and acute medical unit electronic prescribing system with NSAID, triptan and metoclopramide or prochlorperazine as defaults, and require a documented reason before an opioid can be prescribed for a migraine diagnosis.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: same template, next 40 consecutive migraine attendances.
close_loop: Present at ED and neurology governance. If it worked, keep the order set, add opioid use in migraine to the ED prescribing dashboard, and share the pathway with the GP headache service.
evidence: [1321] Surrey elective arthroplasty: protocol-standard analgesia 34% → 61% after an electronic order set (related topic)
[1517] joint replacement: full analgesia protocol compliance 0/27 → 58% after an electronic prescribing order set (related topic)
[2331] post-tonsillectomy analgesia: correct ibuprofen dosing 5% → 55% after a new prescribing guideline with reduced opioids (related topic)
pitfalls: Migraine is under-coded or coded as 'headache' → search both codes and confirm the diagnosis in the notes before including
Clinicians say the triptan or NSAID was contraindicated → record contraindications and report opioid use with and without them
Opioids given before the diagnosis was made → record the time of diagnosis and count only doses given for the migraine
Pushback that patients 'expect' strong analgesia → share the NICE wording and the medication overuse risk, and include re-attendance as a balancing measure
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a neurology or headache nurse as joint leads
Ask pharmacy to run the opioid report for migraine diagnoses; it takes minutes
Give patients a one-page migraine discharge leaflet with triptan advice and medication overuse warning
Track re-attendance within 7 days to show that the change is safe
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from electronic prescribing records

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: In adults seen in neurology clinic with chronic headache, what proportion have the number of days per month they take painkillers or triptans recorded?
why: Medication overuse headache is common and treatable, but it cannot be recognised unless monthly medication days are asked about and recorded. No audit of this has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE CG150 rec 1.2.7 (2012, guideline updated June 2025)
standard.wording: Be alert to the possibility of medication overuse headache in people whose headache developed or worsened while they were taking the following drugs for 3 months or more: triptans, opioids, ergots or combination analgesic medications on 10 days per month or more or paracetamol, aspirin or an NSAID, either alone or in any combination, on 15 days per month or more.

pass: The clinic letter records the number of days per month of acute headache medication use (analgesics, triptans or opioids).
population: Adults (18+) at a new neurology outpatient appointment for headache present on 15 or more days a month. Exclude secondary headache.
sample: 40 consecutive new chronic headache clinic letters over the last 3 months.
data_source: Neurology clinic letters and referral letters.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'Acute medication days per month' line, with the NICE thresholds, to the neurology headache clinic letter template.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: same template, next 40 new chronic headache letters.
close_loop: Present at neurology departmental meeting. If it worked, keep the template line and add it to the GP headache referral form.
evidence: [1207] UK hip fracture discharge letter: correct VTE prophylaxis 87% → 95% after a template prompt (template change; related topic)
pitfalls: Letters say 'uses painkillers frequently' without a number → count only a days-per-month figure as a pass
Consultants use personal templates → agree one shared template line at the department meeting before cycle 2
Referral letters lack the information → add the question to the GP referral form as well
pearls: Ask patients to bring a headache diary to the first visit; the clinic letter invitation can request it
Recruit the headache specialist nurse to champion the template line
Report how many patients met the overuse threshold; it shows the value of asking

area: Older people, stroke, neurology and palliative care
question: In adults with MS who agree to start a disease-modifying therapy, what proportion receive their first dose within 12 weeks of the treatment decision?
why: Early treatment improves long-term outcomes in MS, but screening tests, high-cost drug approval and homecare or infusion set-up can each add weeks after the decision is made. No audit of time to disease-modifying therapy has been published in the library.

standard.source: National Neurosciences Advisory Group, Optimal clinical care pathway for adults: Multiple Sclerosis (2024), Standards and metrics
standard.wording: People with a confirmed diagnosis of MS who are eligible and want to start treatment start DMT within 12 weeks of shared treatment decision

pass: First dose given 84 days or fewer after the documented shared treatment decision.
population: Adults with confirmed MS who agreed to start a first or switched disease-modifying therapy. Exclude people who chose to defer treatment (e.g. pregnancy planning), recorded separately.
sample: All disease-modifying therapy starts in the last 12 months (typically 30–60 in a regional MS service).
data_source: Clinic letters (decision date); pathology system (screening bloods); high-cost drug approval system (e.g. Blueteq); homecare or infusion unit records (first dose).

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–3 collect; Wk 4 analyse/present; Wk 5 change; Wk 6–20 embed; Wk 21–24 re-audit
change: A disease-modifying therapy start checklist in the clinic letter template, so screening bloods, vaccination review and the funding form are all requested at the same appointment as the decision, and a named coordinator tracks each start to first dose.
reaudit: Weeks 21–24: same template, all starts since the change.
close_loop: Present at the MS multidisciplinary meeting and neurology governance. If it worked, keep the checklist and report time to first dose quarterly.
evidence: [2163] Guy's and St Thomas': a dedicated e-referral system cut waits to surgery from 98.2 to 47.7 weeks (system change; related topic)
[5756] UK MS service: treatment of relapses delayed while awaiting urine culture results (related MS pathway delay)
pitfalls: The decision date is unclear in letters → agree before cycle 1 that it is the clinic date when the person agreed to start
Deferred starts inflate delays → record patient-chosen deferral separately and exclude it from the pass rate
Infusion-unit capacity sits outside the MS team → invite the day-unit manager to the results meeting
Small numbers per drug → report overall and by route, not by individual drug
pearls: Recruit the MS nurse or treatment coordinator as co-lead; they hold most of the dates
Chart each step (bloods, funding, homecare, dose) to show where the weeks go
Request screening bloods at the diagnosis visit when treatment is likely
Share the result with the homecare provider; their set-up time is often the longest step
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients across letters, pathology and pharmacy systems
